# The Causal Boundary\chaptersubtitle{From Machine Learning Systems to Physical AI} {#sec-boundary}

![**Systems Stage Focus.** Locator: the five handoffs with this chapter's scope marked](figures/fig_locator.svg){#fig-locator-ch01 fig-pos="H" width=100%}

*Why does an error that costs nothing on a screen destroy hardware in the physical world?*

<!-- HOOK: one substantive paragraph answering the question above. -->

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-objective}
After studying this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Locate the causal boundary in a system description and state what changes on each side of it.
2. Explain why a physical machine violates the independence assumption that underwrites how a model is normally evaluated.
3. Classify a machine into one of the three kinds and predict which physical limit will bind it first.
4. Apply the scope test to a system at the edge of the definition and defend the call.

**Core Chapter Takeaway:** The causal boundary is a structural location, not a matter of degree. Below it, the machine chooses its own next observation, delay is paid in distance, and energy cannot be recalled.

:::

## Introduction {#sec-boundary-1-1}

<!-- SECTION 1.1 -->
<!-- claim: Where computation stops being advice and starts being force, and why that line makes a different kind of engineering. -->
<!-- covers: The structural dividing line of physical AI: crossing from advisory computation (where bad outputs cost compute time or screen pixels) to delegated authority (where outputs command physical force). -->
<!-- covers: The tripartite machine decomposition: a Body governed by mechanics and thermodynamics, a Brain built from learned models, and a Nervous System enforcing temporal deadlines and refusal rights. -->
<!-- covers: Breakdown of classical ML assumptions: why closing the action-perception loop creates non-stationary, endogenous observation streams that violate standard evaluation metrics. -->
<!-- covers: Road map of foundational concepts established in this chapter: the causal boundary register, the three physical machine classes, the four bedrock laws, and the scope test. -->
<!-- GROUNDING: frame — the register write, named as a location rather than measured -->
<!-- FIGURE: A structural block diagram of the tripartite machine showing perception, neural inference, the permission check, and the causal boundary at the actuator register write. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
Every major leap in computing has been defined by the boundary across which bits travel. In personal computing, bits crossed from mainframe backplanes to human eyes through glowing displays. In cloud computing, bits crossed global fiber networks to synchronize distributed databases. In modern generative artificial intelligence, bits traverse deep neural networks to produce text, synthesize imagery, or recommend financial transactions. Yet across all these transformations, one fundamental property of software remained inviolate: the computation lived safely behind glass.

When a digital neural network misclassifies an image in a cloud benchmark, the consequence is confined to an incorrect integer stored in a memory register. When an autoregressive language model generates an ungrounded hallucination, the failure manifests as superfluous text on a browser screen. Software engineers can catch runtime errors, discard invalid outputs, roll back transactions to a clean checkpoint, or rely on human users to ignore an answer. In computer systems engineering, this property is known as idempotency: the state of the surrounding physical universe remains completely decoupled from the intermediate outputs of the software pipeline. Memory can be cleared, registers zeroed, and processes restarted without permanent side effects on the environment.

Physical artificial intelligence begins at the exact instant this isolation breaks. The moment an algorithmic prediction leaves the digital domain to modulate a pulse-width modulation motor drive, fire a valve solenoid, or adjust an electrical grid inverter, computation ceases to be advice and becomes physical force. At this threshold, an unhandled exception is no longer a benign runtime error; it is a burnt motor winding, a sheared gearbox, or a collision with an obstacle in the physical world.

::: {.callout-definition title="Physical AI"}
*Physical AI* is the systems engineering discipline that bridges high-capacity learned models with unyielding physical mechanics, transforming stochastic predictions into dependable, real-time machines that sense, reason, and act in the physical world.
:::

::: {.callout-definition title="The Causal Boundary"}
The *Causal Boundary* is the structural interface where software execution transitions from decoupled information processing to irreversible physical energy exchange.

Crossing this boundary couples computational delay, numerical uncertainty, and algorithmic errors directly to physical state dynamics, momentum, and heat. Advisory systems produce outputs that can be buffered, validated, or discarded without altering the external world, whereas physical systems command actuators whose forces immediately and permanently alter environment state.
:::

A physical artificial intelligence system decomposes structurally into three subsystems that govern this transition. The body consists of the mechanical linkages, structural mass, gearboxes, and power electronics that interact with the physical environment. It does not obey software abstractions, but rather the governing equations of mechanics and thermodynamics, dissipating heat, accumulating mechanical wear, and resisting acceleration through inertia. The brain comprises the learned policies, perception networks, and neural trajectory planners that map incoming sensor streams to candidate actions. Its competence arises from high-dimensional statistical approximation, meaning it cannot provide deterministic guarantees on execution correctness and remains unaccountable for edge cases. Between the two sits the nervous system, the deterministic network fabric and real-time computing platform that carries telemetry, schedules tasks, and evaluates candidate commands. The nervous system enforces the rigid temporal deadlines dictated by the physical dynamics of the body, executes low-latency reflex loops, and retains exclusive authority over safety refusal.

Closing the loop between neural computation and mechanical action breaks the statistical foundations of classical machine learning. Traditional evaluation assumes that data points are independent and identically distributed, drawn from a fixed, exogenous distribution. In a physical machine, every torque command applied to a joint alters the pose of the hardware, shifting camera viewpoints, modifying contact forces, and determining the exact distribution of future sensor observations. The input stream is endogenous, created entirely by the history of actions the machine has already executed. A single erroneous inference does not merely depress a validation score on a static benchmark, but drives the mechanical plant into an unvisited corner of the physical state space. In that unfamiliar regime, the policy exhibits higher variance, producing worse control outputs that push the body further from its training distribution. Because momentum carries the mass forward while the software attempts to recover, computational delay is paid directly in physical displacement.

To build systems capable of surviving these dynamics, engineers must analyze where computation meets mechanics. This chapter establishes that foundation through four central concepts. It isolates the causal boundary at the physical register write, identifying the exact bus transaction where informational reversibility ends and physical consequence begins. It maps the operating space across three distinct classes of physical machines, categorizing hardware by how mechanical dynamics, actuation authority, and recovery envelopes constrain software architecture. It formalizes these constraints into four bedrock laws governing latency, energy, observation causality, and safety refusal. Finally, it introduces a systems scope test that separates physical artificial intelligence from classical robotics and control theory by focusing on what each subsystem costs in time, bandwidth, and energy, and how each component fails under load.
<!-- END -->

## Software That Acts {#sec-boundary-1-2}

<!-- SECTION 1.2 -->
<!-- claim: Advisory software is immune to its own errors because of where it stops, not because of how it was built. -->
<!-- covers: The structural immunity of advisory software: recommenders, classifiers, and chatbots terminate at display buffers or sandboxed APIs where mistakes can be dismissed or undone. -->
<!-- covers: The physical floor of action: tracing computation down to the hardware register (DAC latch, PWM compare register, H-bridge gate driver) whose write transitions a digital value into energy release. -->
<!-- covers: Endogenous observation: formalizing how physical actions alter future state distributions ($s_{t+1} \sim P(\cdot \mid s_t, a_t)$), destroying the i.i.d. assumption underlying offline validation loss. -->
<!-- covers: Delay as distance: deriving why compute and transport latency ($\Delta t$) at velocity ($v$) translates into unalterable spatial displacement ($\Delta x = \int v \, dt$) before corrective action can occur. -->
<!-- covers: The one-way arrow of energy: how electrical, kinetic, or thermal energy transferred to the environment cannot be recalled via software exception handling or transaction rollbacks. -->
<!-- GROUNDING: frame — the register write, named as a location rather than measured -->
<!-- FIGURE: A block diagram contrasting the decoupled dataflow of advisory ML with the closed-loop causal circuit of Physical AI crossing the actuator register boundary. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
Advisory software operates inside an informational container where errors carry negligible physical momentum. When a recommender model serves an irrelevant product, a classifier mislabels an image, or a language model emits an inaccurate token, the computational pipeline terminates in a display buffer, a network socket, or a sandboxed database table. The failure remains bounded by the digital medium. A user dismisses the recommendation, a human analyst closes the alert, or a database transaction coordinator issues an abort that restores memory pages from an undo log. **Advisory software is immune to its own errors because of where it stops, not because of how it was built.** The safety of the pipeline does not stem from statistical guarantees in the training objective or rigorous validation on test splits, but from the physical detachment of the interface. Between the output of the neural network and any change in the physical world, an air gap or a human operator intercepts the signal.

Physical artificial intelligence eliminates that detachment. In a physical machine, the final instruction of a control loop does not write to a screen or populate a web response. It executes a memory-mapped bus transaction that updates a hardware register on an actuator controller. Depending on the machine architecture, that hardware register is a digital-to-analog converter latch holding a commanded reference voltage, a pulse-width modulation compare register setting the duty cycle of a power stage, or a serial control word configuring an H-bridge gate driver. At that exact memory address, informational abstraction ends. The bit pattern written to the register immediately modulates gate voltages across power MOSFETs, drawing current from a DC bus into the copper windings of a motor. Electrical potential converts into magnetic flux, magnetic flux generates mechanical torque across the rotor, and torque accelerates the physical mass of the mechanism.

This transition from digital state to physical force destroys the statistical foundation of classical machine learning. In offline vision, natural language processing, and tabular prediction, data collection is exogenous. The world generates a distribution of inputs $P(x)$, and the model processes them without altering the mechanism that created them. An incorrect classification on sample $i$ has zero effect on the distribution governing sample $i+1$. In a physical system, the environment evolves according to a conditional transition distribution $s_{t+1} \sim P(\cdot \mid s_t, a_t)$, where the next physical state $s_{t+1}$ depends directly on the action $a_t$ produced by the prior model inference. The sensory input stream is endogenous, generated by the machine's own past actions. When a policy produces an erroneous torque command, the joint rotates, the platform shifts, and mounted cameras or lidar units swing into new viewpoints. The machine drives itself into an unfamiliar region of the state space where training data is sparse, increasing the probability of subsequent inference errors and compounding the divergence from nominal operation.

Because physical mass possesses inertia and computation takes finite time, latency in physical AI translates into physical displacement. The time required for photons to strike an image sensor, for frames to traverse a serialized bus, for a neural network to execute tensor contractions, and for a command packet to travel across a controller area network bus constitutes an end-to-end transport and compute latency $\Delta t$. During this delay window, the machine cannot incorporate new sensory information and continues moving along the trajectory dictated by its existing velocity $v(t)$. The resulting unalterable spatial displacement is governed by the integral

$$\Delta x = \int_{0}^{\Delta t} v(t) \, dt$$

As an analytical example, consider a mobile platform traveling at a constant velocity $v = 2.0\text{ m/s}$. If the perception pipeline, neural policy inference, and motor controller communication consume a combined latency $\Delta t = 150\text{ ms}$, the platform traverses $\Delta x = (2.0\text{ m/s}) \times (0.15\text{ s}) = 0.30\text{ m}$ before the first motor response can occur. During those $0.30\text{ m}$, the vehicle is entirely blind to any environmental change that occurred after the initial sensor exposure. If an obstacle enters the path $0.20\text{ m}$ ahead during that inference window, no amount of model capacity or predictive accuracy can alter the outcome, because the physical displacement has already been accumulated by the body.

Once digital commands transition into mechanical work, the state change becomes thermodynamically irreversible. In standard software systems, erroneous mutations are contained through exception handling, memory isolation, and atomic rollback protocols. When an unhandled exception occurs, the runtime unwinds the call stack, reclaims heap allocations, and restores the machine state to a known clean checkpoint. The physical world provides no rollback mechanism. When an actuator controller applies current to a motor, electrical energy transfers from the battery into kinetic energy in mechanical linkages or thermal energy dissipated through resistive heating in the stator windings ($I^2 R$). If an incorrect joint torque drives a manipulator into a rigid steel fixture, the kinetic energy converts into plastic deformation of the tool, mechanical strain on the gearbox teeth, and heat. No software interrupt can pull that kinetic energy out of the crushed structure or restore sheared gear teeth to their original geometry.

The vulnerability of physical AI systems stems from this direct coupling between numerical computation and physical consequence. When an unverified policy output writes directly to an actuator register, informational uncertainty becomes irreversible force. A software pipeline that treats an actuator write as merely another API call ignores the mechanical constraints of momentum, the spatial cost of latency, and the thermodynamic irreversibility of energy transfer. Protecting the physical machine requires a nervous system that sits between the learned model and the actuator register, with the architectural authority to intercept, inspect, and refuse commands before the register latch commits energy to the physical world.
<!-- END -->

## Anatomy of a Crash {#sec-boundary-1-3}

<!-- SECTION 1.3 -->
<!-- claim: The failure was not caused by a bad prediction. It was caused by there being nothing able to refuse one. -->
<!-- covers: Telemetry-backed reconstruction of a physical failure: timestamped step-by-step progression from nominal state to sensor anomaly, inference, register write, and impact. -->
<!-- covers: End-to-end latency budget breakdown: accounting for elapsed time across sensor exposure, bus serialization, neural network forward pass, motor drive latch, and physical inertia. -->
<!-- covers: The direct causal chain: tracing how an out-of-distribution neural prediction passed directly into an actuator register without rate limiting or kinematic bounds checking. -->
<!-- covers: The missing architectural primitive: demonstrating that the control stack lacked an isolated component with the temporal and logical authority to reject an unphysical command vector. -->
<!-- covers: Post-incident telemetry analysis: proving that the learned model functioned strictly within its numerical output space while driving the physical hardware outside its safe operating envelope. -->
<!-- GROUNDING: case — one documented incident, reconstructed from its investigation report -->
<!-- INCIDENT: needs a documented, citable case. Do not invent one. -->
<!-- FIGURE: A synchronized multi-channel telemetry timeline plotting sensor input anomaly, raw model proposal, latched actuator command, and structural envelope violation. -->
<!-- DERIVE: The kinematic stopping distance and time budget required to avert impact compared to the measured end-to-end system latency from the crash telemetry. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
A physical crash in an autonomous machine is rarely caused by an inaccurate prediction alone, but by the absence of an architectural mechanism with the authority to refuse one. On a clear night in March 2018, an automated test vehicle traveling at forty-three miles per hour ($19.2\text{ m/s}$) along a public roadway in Tempe, Arizona, detected an unmodeled obstacle eighty-two meters ahead. Over the next five seconds, the vehicle perception stack repeatedly detected, classified, and reclassified the obstacle across adjacent object categories. Because the perception tracking software associated state filters with discrete semantic labels, each reclassification reset the tracking history and velocity estimate to zero. At $1.2\text{ s}$ before impact, the autonomy software engaged a suppression delay designed to prevent false alarms, allowing the vehicle to travel forward for more than twenty-three meters without deceleration. When the planner finally requested emergency braking at $0.2\text{ s}$ before impact, the remaining physical clearance had collapsed to $3.8\text{ m}$. The vehicle struck the pedestrian at $19.2\text{ m/s}$ without automated deceleration.

Deconstructing the telemetry recorded during the collision reveals a direct chain of timing, classification, and privilege failures. At timestamp $T - 5.6\text{ s}$, the vehicle primary lidar and radar sensors detected an object at a distance of $82.0\text{ m}$, initializing a track in host memory. Between $T - 4.4\text{ s}$ and $T - 1.2\text{ s}$, the stochastic neural classifier toggled its label between a vehicle, a bicycle, and an unclassified obstacle. Because the tracking pipeline wiped historical momentum upon every label transition, the downstream planner never accumulated persistent evidence of an imminent hazard. The neural model functioned strictly within its numerical output space, emitting valid category probabilities and bounding boxes at every forward pass. The failure occurred because the autonomy architecture permitted an unverified, fluctuating perceptual estimate to govern physical authority without independent verification.

The fatal transition from perceptual instability to physical impact was driven by software suppression delays and unbudgeted latency. To mitigate false-positive emergency braking events, the engineering team had inserted a $1.2\text{ s}$ delay between hazard detection and actuator engagement. In digital software, a $1.2\text{ s}$ pause is an invisible scheduling delay; in a vehicle traveling at velocity $v_0 = 19.2\text{ m/s}$, that suppression interval forced the machine to traverse an unalterable reaction distance of

$$d_{\text{react}} = v_0 \times \Delta t_{\text{suppress}} = (19.2\text{ m/s}) \times (1.2\text{ s}) = 23.04\text{ m}$$

During those twenty-three meters, the physical body continued moving forward at full speed while the software deliberated. By the time the autonomy software completed its suppression window and requested emergency braking at $T - 0.2\text{ s}$, the physical distance to the obstacle had closed from $26.8\text{ m}$ to $d_{\text{clear}} = 3.8\text{ m}$. Assuming automotive braking deceleration on dry asphalt of $a_{\max} = 8.0\text{ m/s}^2$, the minimum physical stopping distance required by kinematics evaluates to

$$d_{\text{brake}} = \frac{v_0^2}{2 a_{\max}} = \frac{(19.2\text{ m/s})^2}{2 \times (8.0\text{ m/s}^2)} = 23.04\text{ m}$$

Total stopping distance required $d_{\text{stop}} = d_{\text{react}} + d_{\text{brake}} = 46.08\text{ m}$. Because available clearance was only $3.8\text{ m}$, kinetic impact was mathematically guaranteed two full seconds before the collision occurred.

This investigation autopsy demonstrates why refining perception models or expanding offline training datasets cannot compensate for an architectural absence of authority boundaries. An open-world statistical model will inevitably encounter out-of-distribution scenes, sensor degradations, and transient classification oscillations. The Tempe vehicle crashed not because its neural network was imperfect, but because the autonomy architecture lacked an isolated nervous system running on dedicated real-time silicon with the independent authority to evaluate spatial clearance and execute an emergency stop. If a deterministic safety enforcer had continuously checked the invariant $d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clear}}$ at the hardware floor, the machine would have executed emergency braking at $T - 2.5\text{ s}$, bringing the vehicle to a controlled halt long before available clearance collapsed.
<!-- END -->

## Three Kinds of Physical Machine {#sec-boundary-1-4}

<!-- SECTION 1.4 -->
<!-- claim: Every machine in this book moves mass, applies force through contact, or regulates a flow, and each is bound first by a different limit. -->
<!-- covers: Class 1 (Moving Mass): systems characterized by momentum and spatial displacement where the primary binding floor is stopping distance and kinetic energy dissipation. -->
<!-- covers: Class 2 (Applying Force through Contact): systems characterized by mechanical impedance and surface interaction where the primary binding floor is actuator torque and structural stiffness. -->
<!-- covers: Class 3 (Regulating Continuous Flow): systems characterized by thermodynamics and fluid transport where the primary binding floor is thermal capacity and mass conservation. -->
<!-- covers: The first-exhausted physical budget: determining for any machine whether spatial clearance, structural stress, or heat dissipation creates the critical deadline. -->
<!-- covers: The book's running tri-machine testbed: introducing the three standardized reference systems that anchor worked derivations and telemetry across all subsequent chapters. -->
<!-- GROUNDING: frame — three machine classes, each with the limit that binds it first -->
<!-- FIGURE: A comparative reference chart mapping the three machine classes to their governing conservation laws, primary actuator interfaces, and first binding physical limits. -->
<!-- DERIVE: The first-order stopping distance $d = \frac{v^2}{2a_{\max}}$ and thermal rise rate $\frac{dT}{dt} = \frac{P_{\text{in}} - P_{\text{out}}}{C_{\text{th}}}$ as the physical floors bounding mass and flow architectures. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
Every machine governed by a learned policy falls into one of three structural classes based on the physical quantity its actuators manipulate. A machine either moves mass across space, applies mechanical force through physical contact, or regulates the continuous flow of a thermal or fluid medium (@fig-three-archetypes). While software architectures across these systems run identical tensor runtimes and linear algebra accelerators, their execution domains cannot share a single safety invariant or timing deadline. Each class is governed by a distinct physical conservation law that dictates which budget is exhausted first when an inference runtime stalls or produces an unphysical output.

![**The Three Canonical Archetypes of Physical AI.** (a) Mobility: Autonomous legged, wheeled, and aerial platforms navigating continuous space under kinetic momentum constraints. (b) Contact Manipulation: Articulated linkages and dexterous hands interacting with stiff environments under high contact impedance. (c) Cybernetic Energy and Processes: Grid-scale power inverters and fluid loops governing sub-millisecond electrical switching and thermodynamic flows.](figures/fig01_three_archetypes.jpg){#fig-three-archetypes width=100%}

Class 1 machines move mass across space, and their execution is bound first by momentum and kinetic energy dissipation. In autonomous transport platforms, mobile manipulators, and aerial vehicles, the actuator bridge applies force to translate or rotate a body with mass $m$ at velocity $v$. Because kinetic energy $E_k = \frac{1}{2}m v^2$ cannot be recalled once delivered to the chassis, safety is measured as remaining spatial clearance. When braking begins at maximum allowable deceleration $a_{\max}$, the physical floor for stopping distance follows the kinematic relation $d = \frac{v^2}{2a_{\max}}$. Consider an analytical example of a warehouse transport robot with mass $m = 120\text{ kg}$ traveling at $v = 2.0\text{ m/s}$. If wheel traction limits deceleration to $a_{\max} = 4.0\text{ m/s}^2$, the minimum physical distance required to arrest the vehicle is $d = \frac{(2.0\text{ m/s})^2}{2 \times 4.0\text{ m/s}^2} = 0.50\text{ m}$. If the nervous system introduces an end-to-end sensing and inference delay of $t_{\text{lag}} = 150\text{ ms}$, the chassis traverses an additional $v t_{\text{lag}} = 0.30\text{ m}$ before braking torque develops, yielding a total stopping requirement of $0.80\text{ m}$. In a mass-moving system, latency converts directly into spatial displacement, and the first boundary breached during a software stall is the distance to an external obstacle.

Class 2 machines apply mechanical force through contact, where the primary binding limit is actuator torque and structural stiffness. In articulated industrial arms, robotic assembly fixtures, and surgical tools, the end-effector interacts directly with a rigid or compliant workpiece. Unlike a mobile platform operating in open space, an arm in contact with a surface cannot resolve an unexpected displacement command by rolling forward. When an actuator commands position into a rigid boundary, displacement is constrained and the interaction is governed by mechanical impedance. By Hooke law, the contact force generated by a spatial penetration error $\Delta x$ against an environment of stiffness $k$ is $F = k \Delta x$. If a learned policy produces an analytical position error of $\Delta x = 2.0\text{ mm}$ against an assembly fixture with stiffness $k = 5.0 \times 10^5\text{ N/m}$, contact force rises by $1000\text{ N}$ within the time required for stress waves to propagate through the tooling. If the nervous system fails to clamp motor current within milliseconds, the motor drives the gear train past its shear limit or damages the workpiece. The critical floor in contact systems is not stopping distance, but the time rate of force rise $\frac{dF}{dt}$ relative to actuator current loop bandwidth and structural yield stress.

Class 3 machines regulate continuous fluid or thermal flow, where the primary binding limit is thermal capacity and mass conservation. In chemical batch reactors, liquid cooling loops for compute clusters, and battery thermal management plants, actuators manipulate pumps, valves, and heating elements rather than mechanical linkages. The state of the system is governed by mass transport and energy balance rather than kinematics. For a thermal system with lumped heat capacity $C_{\text{th}}$, the rate of temperature change obeys the first-order differential equation $\frac{dT}{dt} = \frac{P_{\text{in}} - P_{\text{out}}}{C_{\text{th}}}$, where $P_{\text{in}}$ is the thermal power added to the fluid and $P_{\text{out}}$ is the heat removed by active circulation. Consider an analytical battery module with thermal capacity $C_{\text{th}} = 800\text{ J/K}$ generating $P_{\text{in}} = 2400\text{ W}$ under fast charging. If a control failure closes the coolant valve such that $P_{\text{out}} = 0\text{ W}$, the temperature rise rate becomes $\frac{dT}{dt} = \frac{2400\text{ W}}{800\text{ J/K}} = 3.0\text{ K/s}$. If cell chemistry permits an overtemperature margin of $\Delta T = 15\text{ K}$ before thermal runaway becomes irreversible, the system exhausts its safety budget in $t = \frac{15\text{ K}}{3.0\text{ K/s}} = 5.0\text{ s}$. The deadline in flow architectures is set by thermal capacitance and transport delay, providing a longer temporal window than mechanics but one where energy accumulation cannot be quickly reversed once started.

For any physical AI system, engineering the nervous system begins by determining which physical budget is exhausted first during a failure. In software systems, resource constraints center on processor cycles, memory allocation, and network bandwidth. In physical systems, the engineer must identify whether spatial clearance, structural stress, or heat dissipation creates the critical timing deadline. In a high-speed vehicle, spatial clearance fails within fractions of a second while motor winding temperatures remain safely below thermal limits. In an assembly press, mechanical stress exceeds the yield point of structural members within tens of milliseconds long before the chassis moves perceptibly or heats up. In a chemical reactor, mechanical stress is negligible, but accumulated thermal energy breaches safe operational envelopes over several seconds. The shortest time to failure across these three domains defines the deterministic execution deadline that the nervous system must meet.

To evaluate architectural tradeoffs across these distinct physical domains, this book grounds its derivations and telemetry in three standardized reference machines. The first reference system is an autonomous warehouse transport robot, representing Class 1. It features a $120\text{ kg}$ differential-drive chassis equipped with optical wheel encoders and planar lidar, operating under traction limits and momentum constraints. The second reference system is a six-axis articulated industrial manipulator, representing Class 2. It features direct-drive joint actuators with strain-gauge torque sensors, performing high-speed pick-and-place and precision contact insertion against rigid assembly jigs. The third reference system is an industrial liquid thermal regulation plant, representing Class 3. It features variable-speed coolant pumps, proportional control valves, and heat exchangers managing thermal dissipation for a high-wattage compute rack.

Every architectural pattern in subsequent chapters (from shared memory layout to deterministic referee logic) is evaluated against the physical parameters of these three reference platforms. While their mechanical designs, fluid properties, and actuator interfaces require distinct domain models, the constraints that bind them originate from a shared set of physical principles.
<!-- END -->

## The Four Bedrock Laws {#sec-boundary-1-5}

<!-- SECTION 1.5 -->
<!-- claim: Four properties recur in every physical machine regardless of what it is built from or what model it runs. -->
<!-- covers: Law 1 (Irreversibility of Physical Action): Energy deposited into the environment is thermodynamically irreversible; software rollbacks cannot un-apply force or retrieve kinetic energy. -->
<!-- covers: Law 2 (Information Age and Delay-as-Distance): A sensor measurement describes the past; during inference and transport latency, the physical world continues to evolve along its uncontrolled trajectory. -->
<!-- covers: Law 3 (Separation of Proposal and Permission): The subsystem generating complex behavior (the learned model) must never hold unmediated permission to write to physical actuator registers. -->
<!-- covers: Law 4 (Evidentiary Release): Safe deployment cannot be justified by average-case empirical validation loss, but requires formal bounding envelopes verified against worst-case physics. -->
<!-- covers: Universal manifestation: demonstrating how all four bedrock laws govern mass, contact, and flow systems equally despite their differing mechanical embodiments. -->
<!-- GROUNDING: frame — four properties, each derived from the crash just read -->
<!-- FIGURE: A matrix mapping each of the four bedrock laws to its physical mechanism, mathematical formulation, and concrete failure mode across the three machine classes. -->
<!-- DERIVE: The state uncertainty growth envelope $\Delta x(\tau) \le \int_0^\tau v(t) dt + \frac{1}{2} a_{\max} \tau^2$ as a direct function of sensor-to-actuation age $\tau$. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
Four bedrock laws govern every machine whose nervous system translates compute cycles into physical action. These properties are not specific to a single kinematic configuration or software framework. They arise whenever a digital controller interacts with physical reality across the causal boundary. Whether an architecture accelerates a wheeled chassis, applies contact torque with a robotic arm, or pumps liquid coolant through a heat exchanger, the machine operates under constraints imposed by thermodynamics, transport delay, actuator isolation, and verification physics.

::: {.callout-law title="1. The Law of Physical Causality and Irreversibility"}
Software state can be caught with an exception block, isolated in a virtual container, or restored from a checkpoint. Physical actions ($W_t \to W_{t+1}$) governed by mass, inertia, friction, and gravity are permanent and irreversible. Every actuation permanently alters the physical environment, dissipates energy, and alters all future sensory observations endogenously ($a_t \to u(t) \to W_{t+1} \to o_{t+1}$).
:::

The first bedrock law is the thermodynamic irreversibility of physical action. In a pure software system, an erroneous operation is reversed by rolling back a database transaction, restoring a file from a snapshot, or restarting a process with clean memory. In a physical machine, an actuator converts electrical charge into kinetic energy, structural strain, or fluid pressure. Once that energy crosses the causal boundary into the environment, it cannot be recalled. When an erroneous command accelerates a $120\text{ kg}$ warehouse robot toward an obstacle, the kinetic energy deposited into the chassis can only be counteracted by applying opposing forces through friction brakes, which dissipates the energy as heat. If an over-current command drives a six-axis manipulator into an assembly jig, the mechanical stress exceeds the yield point of the metal within $15\text{ ms}$, permanently deforming the tooling. Software transactions can be rolled back, but thermodynamic work cannot be undone.

::: {.callout-law title="2. The Law of Information Freshness (The Time Law)"}
The physical world does not pause while an artificial intelligence model computes. Sensor observations age the microsecond photons strike the photodiode or acoustic waves reach a transducer. Mean latency ($P_{50}$) is an illusion; tail latency ($P_{99}$), memory bus contention, and information age ($\Delta t$) dictate physical closed-loop stability and dynamic stopping distances ($d_{\text{stop}}$).
:::

The second bedrock law is the equivalence of information age and spatial displacement. Every sensor measurement describes the past. Photons strike an image sensor, strain gauges change resistance, and pressure transducers generate voltages, but converting these physical phenomena into memory buffers and transporting them across an interconnect requires time. By the time a neural network completes inference and emits an action vector, the state of the world has evolved along an uncontrolled trajectory during the latency interval $\tau$.

During this latency interval, unobserved forces and ongoing motion expand the uncertainty of the machine true state. For a machine operating with current velocity $v(t)$ and subject to unmodeled external accelerations or disturbance forces bounded by $a_{\max}$, the state uncertainty growth envelope $\Delta x(\tau)$ as a direct function of total sensor-to-actuation age $\tau$ obeys the analytical bound

$$\Delta x(\tau) \le \int_0^\tau v(t) \, dt + \frac{1}{2} a_{\max} \tau^2$$

Consider an analytical example using a warehouse robot traveling at an initial velocity $v_0 = 1.5\text{ m/s}$. If floor grade or wheel slip introduces an unmodeled acceleration bounded by $a_{\max} = 2.0\text{ m/s}^2$, an inference and communication delay of $\tau = 200\text{ ms}$ produces a positional uncertainty envelope of $\Delta x \le (1.5)(0.200) + 0.5(2.0)(0.200)^2 = 0.340\text{ m}$. If the robot operates within $0.200\text{ m}$ of a pallet rack, collision is guaranteed before the computed action reaches the motor drive. In an industrial manipulator operating at an end-effector speed of $0.8\text{ m/s}$ near a rigid boundary, a $50\text{ ms}$ bus stall creates a $40\text{ mm}$ displacement uncertainty, which exceeds the structural deflection limit of the workpiece by an order of magnitude. In a physical system, latency is an uncontrolled displacement in physical space rather than an idle wait state.

::: {.callout-law title="3. The Law of Proposal–Permission Privilege (The Architecture Law)"}
No stochastic, learned neural network (such as a vision-language-action model or diffusion policy) may hold direct motor authority. Learned models running on application processors are untrusted proposal services. Real-time physical permission belongs exclusively to dedicated, zero-allocation microcontrollers running deterministic mathematical safety envelopes and physical fallbacks.
:::

The third bedrock law requires strict separation between proposal and permission. The subsystem of the nervous system that generates complex, goal-directed behavior operates by optimization over high-dimensional learned representations. Because deep neural networks are uninterpretable and produce erratic outputs under out-of-distribution inputs, a learned policy must never hold direct write access to physical actuator registers. If an unconstrained model can directly set pulse-width modulation duty cycles or valve drive currents, an unexpected visual reflection or floating-point anomaly will drive hardware into physical limits. The role of the learned model is strictly to propose candidate trajectories. The authority to grant permission, clip commands to safe physical envelopes, or reject the proposed action entirely must belong to a separate, deterministic supervisory layer running on isolated execution hardware.

::: {.callout-law title="4. The Law of Governed Change and Defensible Release (The Safety Law)"}
A physical agent shapes its own future data distribution. Naive training on raw operational logs without isolating safety interventions induces severe covariate shift and policy collapse. A cherry-picked video demonstration is not evidence of safety; defensible release requires cross-layer fault injection and a formal safety case rendering an accountable release verdict.
:::

The fourth bedrock law dictates that deployment readiness cannot be justified by empirical validation loss. In cloud computing, software reliability is evaluated statistically. An engineer measures mean accuracy, accepts an uptime target of $P_{99.9}$, and resolves rare corner-case crashes through automated restarts and rolling updates. In physical AI, the tail of the error distribution manifests as mechanical destruction. A learned policy that achieves a $P_{99.99}$ success rate on an offline test benchmark fails once every $10{,}000$ control steps. In a system running a $50\text{ Hz}$ control loop, that error rate produces a physical failure every $200\text{ s}$ of continuous operation. Safe operation cannot be certified by average-case performance metrics gathered over finite training sets. It requires formal, worst-case envelope bounds verified against the physical laws of the plant, ensuring that even if the learned proposal violates safety limits, the machine remains within guaranteed physical boundaries.

These four bedrock laws govern mass, contact, and flow systems equally, regardless of their mechanical domain. In a Class 1 warehouse robot, irreversibility governs momentum, delay consumes stopping distance, proposal separation protects wheel traction limits, and worst-case bounds prevent chassis collisions. In a Class 2 industrial manipulator, irreversibility governs plastic deformation, delay consumes spatial clearances against rigid jigs, proposal separation prevents joint torque spikes, and worst-case bounds prevent structural yielding. In a Class 3 thermal regulation plant, irreversibility governs thermal energy accumulation, delay creates temperature overshoots past thermal sensor lag, proposal separation prevents pump cavitation, and worst-case bounds prevent coolant boiling. In every case, safe physical operation requires that the authority to execute an action remains decoupled from the process that conceived it.
<!-- END -->

## Proposal and Permission {#sec-boundary-1-6}

<!-- SECTION 1.6 -->
<!-- claim: Authority over actuation must belong to something that can refuse even when the proposer is broken. -->
<!-- covers: The unprivileged proposer principle: treating the neural network strictly as an untrusted advisory generator of candidate actions rather than an actuator driver. -->
<!-- covers: The independent permission authority: defining the deterministic, bounded-execution gate (the nervous system reflex/enforcer) that intercepts proposals before register latching. -->
<!-- covers: Asymmetric failure tolerance: why the permission gate must maintain system safety even when the proposer crashes, hangs, outputs NaNs, or encounters out-of-distribution state. -->
<!-- covers: The mechanics of refusal: defining safe intervention strategies including rate clamping, envelope clipping, braking, and graceful fallback trajectory execution. -->
<!-- covers: Architectural boundary: why safety constraints cannot be enforced via training-time loss penalties or reward shaping, but must exist as hard downstream architectural gates. -->
<!-- GROUNDING: frame — the proposer and the authority, as an idea with no silicon -->
<!-- FIGURE: A control-flow diagram showing the untrusted Brain proposing a trajectory to the independent Nervous System gate which checks physical invariants before register commit. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
Authority over actuation must belong to a mechanism that can refuse execution even when the proposer is broken. This separation between proposal and permission is a structural principle that exists prior to any choice of silicon, bus topology, or register layout. In a pure software system, an unprivileged process can be granted direct write access to application memory because an erroneous write costs only compute cycles and memory bandwidth to correct. In a physical machine, state changes move mass, dissipate heat, and expend momentum that cannot be recalled. Because a learned policy is an inductive statistical model whose worst-case outputs under distribution shift cannot be mathematically bounded, the neural network must function strictly as an unprivileged proposer. The policy evaluates sensory history and suggests candidate control actions, such as target joint torques, steering angles, or valve duty cycles, but it holds zero direct authority over the physical plant. Routing learned model outputs directly to actuator registers couples the mechanical integrity of the machine to the unverified tail of a probability distribution.

Training-time optimization cannot substitute for runtime invariant enforcement. In reinforcement learning and imitation learning pipelines, developers frequently attempt to enforce safety by augmenting the objective function with penalty terms, barrier losses, or negative reward shaping. These numerical penalties influence gradient descent during training, reducing the empirical frequency of undesirable states across the training distribution. They provide no guarantees at runtime. When the deployed policy encounters novel sensor noise, lens occlusion, or out-of-distribution state combinations, the offline optimization cannot prevent the network from generating an unsafe control vector. Soft optimization incentives shape probability distributions, but physical safety requires deterministic boundary enforcement. Safety constraints must therefore live downstream of the model as an explicit, hard architectural gate positioned between the policy output and the actuator registers.

The permission authority is a deterministic, bounded-execution gate that evaluates candidate proposals against physical invariants before register latching. Implemented within the nervous system layer, this gate executes in fixed, predictable time on isolated compute resources. Its function is not to invent alternative tasks or optimize high-level objectives, but to verify whether executing the proposed command preserves the safety invariants of the physical body. For an articulated industrial arm, the authority evaluates whether the proposed acceleration profile violates joint torque limits, whether the projected velocity leaves sufficient braking margin before mechanical hardstops, and whether the swept kinematic volume intersects static workcell geometry. If the proposed command satisfies all physical constraints, the gate grants permission and latches the values into the digital-to-analog converters or motor driver registers. If any invariant is violated, the gate denies execution immediately.

System safety must be asymmetric with respect to the proposer, remaining guaranteed even when the learned model fails completely. A learned policy can fail in failure modes that cannot be modeled statistically. The inference accelerator can experience a thermal throttle or bus deadlock, the neural network can output floating-point NaNs or infinities due to a numerical underflow in an attention layer, or the policy can enter high-frequency limit cycles when exposed to optical glare. The permission gate must treat the proposer as an untrusted, potentially adversarial signal source. In an analytical system running a $100\text{ Hz}$ control loop with a $10\text{ ms}$ deadline, the permission authority monitors heartbeat signals, numerical validity, and latency bounds on every cycle. If the proposer fails to deliver a valid, finite control vector within its allotted $8\text{ ms}$ compute budget, the gate registers a proposer failure and executes a deterministic safety response without waiting for the inference process to recover.

When a candidate action is refused, the permission authority must execute a deterministic intervention strategy that maintains the physical machine within its safe operating envelope. Refusal cannot consist of simply dropping the command and allowing actuator registers to float. If a mobile base moving at $2.0\text{ m/s}$ suddenly receives zero motor current without controlled deceleration, momentum drives the unconstrained mass into obstacles or induces wheel slip that invalidates odometry. The permission authority applies a graded hierarchy of interventions matched to the severity of the violation. For minor envelope exceedances, the gate applies projection or rate clamping, mapping the candidate vector to the nearest point on the boundary of the admissible control set. For kinematically hazardous proposals, the gate clips the command to maximum allowable jerk and acceleration envelopes. When the proposer suffers a total failure or proposes a trajectory that breaches fundamental physical invariants, the permission authority bypasses the model entirely and engages a deterministic fallback controller, commanding controlled regenerative braking or following a verified deceleration trajectory to bring the mass to a stationary, passive state.

By placing the causal boundary of authority downstream of the learned model, the physical AI architecture isolates the unpredictable dynamics of statistical inference from the deterministic physics of the plant. The brain remains free to perform complex perception and open-world reasoning, while the nervous system guarantees that no command reaching the body can violate physical limits. This structural decoupling establishes the baseline mechanism upon which all operational guarantees must be built, separating the generation of intelligent behavior from the non-negotiable enforcement of physical safety.
<!-- END -->

## Safety, Security, and Accountability {#sec-boundary-1-7}

<!-- SECTION 1.7 -->
<!-- claim: Three different questions, one mechanism. Safety asks whether the machine did harm. Security asks whether someone else made it. Accountability asks whether anyone can say afterwards what happened and why. -->
<!-- covers: Safety as non-adversarial failure: hazards arising when stochastic physical dynamics, component wear, or distribution shifts cause an unrefused hazardous proposal. -->
<!-- covers: Security as adversarial failure: hazards arising when an external attacker exploits sensor spoofing, network injection, or adversarial inputs to command hazardous physical force. -->
<!-- covers: Accountability as deterministic auditability: high-rate, tamper-evident telemetry capture at the causal boundary proving what the model proposed, what the gate permitted, and why. -->
<!-- covers: The unified authority primitive: demonstrating that safety, security, and accountability all resolve to whether an independent authority possessed the capability and state to refuse a register write. -->
<!-- covers: Physical authority delegation vs software ACLs: why traditional capability-based security models must be extended to account for momentum, continuous state, and physical dynamics. -->
<!-- GROUNDING: frame — three questions, shown to reduce to one -->
<!-- FIGURE: A unified architectural model demonstrating how Safety, Security, and Accountability converge on the single physical authority enforcement point at the causal boundary. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
Safety asks whether the machine caused harm. Security asks whether an external agent forced it to. Accountability asks whether an auditor can determine afterwards what occurred and why. In software services, these three concerns belong to separate engineering organizations and distinct runtimes, dividing along application logic, network firewalls, and audit logging databases. In a machine that moves mass and commands current, all three questions collapse into a single physical primitive at the causal boundary, determining whether an independent gate possessed the state and the authority to refuse a register write before torque reached the plant.

Safety failures arise without an adversary. A camera lens accumulates dust over $500\text{ h}$ of operation, shifting the input distribution away from the training domain until an attention head generates an out-of-distribution steering torque. A joint bearing develops mechanical play, introducing unmodeled compliance that converts a stable learned position trajectory into a resonant limit cycle. Or a sudden change in surface friction drops tire traction below the friction coefficient assumed by the learned policy. In each case, the proposer generates an action that is statistically plausible to the network but physically hazardous to the body. If the permission gate lacks the independent kinematic model or thermal budget to detect the exceedance, the unrefused command writes to the motor drive registers, and stored kinetic energy is released into the workspace.

Security failures introduce an adversary who deliberately exploits the gap between statistical inference and physical reality. An attacker does not need to compromise cryptographic keys or gain root access on the host operating system if they can manipulate sensory inputs. Projected structured light can spoof a depth sensor, acoustic injection can resonate MEMS gyroscopes at their resonant frequency of $27\text{ kHz}$ to corrupt inertial odometry, or adversarial visual perturbations on a factory floor can induce a vision-language-action model to output maximum actuator velocity. On a traditional server, an injection attack compromises data confidentiality or integrity within an abstract memory space. In physical AI, an injection attack commands physical work, turning an unvalidated inference into mechanical force. The security perimeter cannot terminate at the network interface or the operating system system-call boundary. It terminates at the permission gate, which must evaluate every candidate command against physical invariants regardless of whether the proposer acted in good faith or under adversarial control.

Traditional software authorization models fail in physical machines because capability tokens and access control lists assume discrete, memoryless transactions. In a web service, possessing a valid credential grants permission to write a record to a database, and the cost of the operation is bounded by compute cycles and storage bytes. In physical space, permission is not a static binary entitlement. In an analytical robotic joint, a command to apply $50\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ of torque is valid when the link is stationary at mid-stroke, but the identical command causes structural yield if the joint is $2\text{ mm}$ from its hard stop moving at $1.5\text{ rad/s}$. Physical authority is state-dependent, continuous, and dynamic, governed by velocity, momentum, thermal accumulation, and spatial occupancy. A permission gate cannot evaluate an action in isolation as a stateless remote procedure call. It must integrate the action over time against the current physical state of the body, validating that the integral of applied forces remains within the invariant reachable set of the plant.

Accountability requires proving the exact causal chain that led to actuation when a machine damages hardware or breaches an envelope. In standard computing systems, logging is asynchronous, best-effort, and coarse-grained, dropping records during buffer pressure or recording timestamps with millisecond jitter. At the causal boundary, accountability demands deterministic, high-rate telemetry captured synchronously with the control loop. If a joint actuator commands $1000\text{ Hz}$ updates with a $1\text{ ms}$ deadline, the permission gate must record the raw candidate vector proposed by the model, the state estimate used by the gate, the mathematical criterion applied by the safety filter, and the exact vector written to the hardware registers. Sealing these records in tamper-evident, append-only circular buffers provides post-incident reconstruction. When an accident occurs, an engineer can verify mathematically whether the failure originated in a corrupted sensor reading, a degraded policy proposal, an erroneous permission rule, or a mechanical component that failed to produce the commanded counter-torque.

Safety, security, and accountability converge on the single physical authority enforcement point at the causal boundary. Safety verifies that the proposed command obeys physical invariants. Security ensures that no unauthenticated or adversarial proposal can bypass those invariants to command actuator current. Accountability records the state and rationale of the decision before the energy leaves the nervous system. If the permission gate is structurally independent, running on isolated compute with direct hardware interlocks, all three guarantees hold simultaneously. If the permission gate is bypassed, coupled to the inference engine, or omitted, all three guarantees collapse together, regardless of how many software security layers or safety guidelines surround the model. The division between systems that require this architectural discipline and those that do not is not a matter of model scale or sensor count. It is defined by the physical consequences of unrefused authority.
<!-- END -->

## The Scope Test {#sec-boundary-1-8}

<!-- SECTION 1.8 -->
<!-- claim: Three conditions together define the subject, and feedback alone is not one of them. -->
<!-- covers: The three joint criteria for Physical AI: a learned component (unspecifiable policy), consequential physical feedback (action alters next state), and delegated physical authority (automated actuator writes). -->
<!-- covers: Why feedback loops alone are insufficient: distinguishing Physical AI from classical fixed-gain PID control (no learned policy) and digital algorithmic trading (no physical feedback). -->
<!-- covers: Why learned models alone are insufficient: distinguishing Physical AI from offline trajectory optimizers and diagnostic vision models (no delegated physical authority). -->
<!-- covers: Systems satisfying exactly two criteria: evaluating edge cases such as real-time driver alert monitors (no authority), analog thermostats (no learned model), and automated stock trading (no physical feedback). -->
<!-- covers: The borderline case: human-in-the-loop teleoperation with learned assistance, where physical authority is shared dynamically between human and model. -->
<!-- covers: The decisive boundary test: a step-by-step decision rubric for evaluating ambiguous systems at the interface of computation and the physical world. -->
<!-- GROUNDING: frame — the scope test applied to cases at the edge -->
<!-- FIGURE: A three-set Venn diagram defining the scope of Physical AI at the intersection of Learned Models, Physical Feedback, and Delegated Authority, with edge systems plotted in each region. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
Three conditions together define Physical AI, and feedback alone is not one of them. The scope of this discipline is not determined by model parameter counts, compute budgets, or the mere attachment of an electric motor to a microcontroller. It is defined by the simultaneous intersection of three structural criteria. The machine must contain a learned component whose policy mapping is acquired from data rather than specified analytically. It must experience consequential physical feedback, where an executed action alters the physical state of the environment and governs what the sensors observe next under the laws of mechanics and thermodynamics. It must possess delegated physical authority, where automated software routines write directly to actuator registers without synchronous human approval in the control loop. If any one of these three conditions is absent, the machine belongs to an established engineering discipline with different failure modes, different verification methods, and different safety guarantees. Only when all three converge does a machine operate under the failure dynamics where software latency converts directly into kinetic damage.

A closed feedback loop is necessary for physical interaction, but feedback alone does not place a machine in this domain. Classical proportional-integral-derivative controllers run at $1000\text{ Hz}$ across aerospace and industrial automation, regulating valve positions and motor torques through tight sensory feedback. Their feedback loops are continuous and physical, but their control laws are specified entirely by fixed mathematical formulas whose stability bounds can be proven analytically from transfer functions. They hold physical authority and experience physical feedback, but they lack a learned model. Conversely, high-frequency algorithmic trading engines execute automated market orders under learned predictive models within microseconds. They combine learned policies with delegated transactional authority, but the feedback they receive is purely digital and informational. When an order executes, it alters an electronic order book rather than momentum, friction, or thermal energy. An unhandled stall in algorithmic trading costs financial capital, but it does not cause an inertia-driven collision with a structural fixture.

A learned model is equally insufficient on its own to define the field. Modern engineering workflows frequently deploy deep neural networks to optimize robot trajectories offline or inspect manufactured parts on assembly lines. An offline neural trajectory optimizer may compute time-optimal paths for a six-axis robotic manipulator over several seconds of cluster compute, but if that trajectory is verified by an engineer or executed through a classical deterministic controller with hard-coded envelope stops, the learned model holds no delegated physical authority over the plant. Similarly, a convolutional neural network monitoring an assembly line may classify surface defects at $60\text{ frames/s}$. If the classification output merely logs an entry in a database or flags a display for a human operator, the model operates outside the causal loop. A false negative or an inference timeout produces a corrupted record, but it cannot directly command an actuator to over-torque a mechanical joint.

Systems that satisfy exactly two criteria demonstrate where the structural boundary lies. A real-time driver drowsiness monitor uses a learned computer vision model to track eyelid movement and vehicle lane position, receiving continuous physical feedback from the vehicle state. Yet it lacks delegated physical authority because its only output is an auditory warning chime. If the vision model fails completely during an inference stall, the speaker emits no sound, but the steering rack and brake calipers remain under human control. An analog bimetallic thermostat possesses delegated physical authority over a gas furnace valve and operates in continuous feedback with the thermal mass of a building, but its transfer function is a fixed thermodynamic property of two bonded metals rather than a learned representation. An automated trading bot possesses both a learned policy and delegated execution authority, but its actions propagate through network packets and databases without interacting with the physical laws of mass and motion.

The most demanding edge cases occur in shared autonomy, where physical authority is divided dynamically between a human operator and a learned model. In robotic surgery or advanced driver assistance, a human operator provides continuous steering or tool guidance while a learned policy injects corrections to filter hand tremors, avoid anatomical boundaries, or compensate for vehicle slip. These architectures satisfy both the learned component and physical feedback criteria. Whether they fall within the scope of Physical AI depends strictly on the temporal authority granted to the model. If the learned policy can command even $2.0\text{ N}$ of force or adjust steering angle without requiring human confirmation within the $200\text{ ms}$ threshold of human reflex latency, the model possesses delegated physical authority. During that $200\text{ ms}$ window, an erroneous model output or a delayed inference packet acts on the physical world before the operator can intercede.

Evaluating an ambiguous machine requires a three-step decision rubric that tests each criterion independently. The first test determines whether the system contains a policy component whose mapping is learned from data rather than specified analytically in closed form. If it does not, the machine belongs to classical control theory. The second test determines whether actuator commands alter a physical plant such that subsequent sensor observations are governed by mechanics, thermodynamics, or fluid dynamics. If they do not, the machine is a digital machine learning system. The third test determines whether the learned component writes commands to physical actuators without a human supervisor or an independent deterministic barrier capable of vetoing the action before physical momentum accumulates. If it does not, the machine is an offline decision-support tool. When all three tests pass, the system operates as Physical AI, and its engineering must be governed by the laws of the causal boundary.
<!-- END -->

## Systems Stress-Tests {#sec-boundary-1-9}

<!-- SECTION 1.9 -->
<!-- claim: Systems that satisfy two of the three conditions expose where the definition does real work. -->
<!-- covers: Systems with learned models and physical feedback but zero actuation authority (e.g., real-time driver alert systems and medical diagnostic monitors). -->
<!-- covers: Systems with physical feedback and delegated authority but no learned components (e.g., flyball governors, analog thermostats, and classical avionics autopilots). -->
<!-- covers: Systems with learned models and delegated authority over digital state rather than physical mass (e.g., autonomous high-frequency market-making algorithms). -->
<!-- covers: The borderline case: human-in-the-loop teleoperation with learned assistance, where authority is shared dynamically between human and model. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
To transition from conceptual definitions to whole-system architectural reasoning, consider four foundational dilemmas where systems that satisfy two of the three criteria expose where the boundary of Physical AI does real work.

#### Stress-Test 1: The Advisory Observer (Learned Model and Physical Feedback, Zero Authority) {.unnumbered}

**The Scenario.** An advanced driver assistance monitor uses an onboard neural network to process high-resolution camera streams, detecting highway lane boundaries and surrounding traffic. When the vehicle drifts toward a lane marking without a turn signal, the system sounds an audible warning buzzer and illuminates an LED indicator on the dashboard. The system has no electrical connection to the steering rack or brake actuators.

**The Digital versus Physical Contrast.** In a software evaluation, an ML engineer treats the warning chime as the complete system deliverable, celebrating a $99.5\%$ detection accuracy on validation benchmarks. In the physical world, the vehicle continues moving at $30.0\text{ m/s}$ ($108\text{ km/h}$) along its uncorrected trajectory because an audible alert possesses zero mechanical authority to arrest kinetic momentum.

**The Systems Dilemma.** First, if an alert system achieves near-perfect classification accuracy but the human driver suffers a cognitive distraction delay of $1.5\text{ s}$, the vehicle traverses $45.0\text{ m}$ of unguided displacement before physical intervention begins. Why does isolating the software from actuator registers place the failure domain entirely within human ergonomics rather than physical systems engineering? Second, what architectural hardware boundary guarantees that a firmware update or software bug cannot accidentally grant the advisory perception task write-access to the electronic power steering bus? Third, why does the absence of delegated authority allow this system to be verified through offline statistical datasets without requiring hardware-in-the-loop physical crash testing?

**The Physical AI Insight.** Without delegated physical authority, computational errors remain safely behind glass. The machine operates as a decision-support tool, and physical safety is defended entirely by human physiology.

#### Stress-Test 2: The Fast Deterministic Governor (Physical Feedback and Delegated Authority, No Learning) {.unnumbered}

**The Scenario.** A high-performance quadrotor drone executes an acrobatic attitude stabilization maneuver using a proportional-integral-derivative flight controller running at $1000\text{ Hz}$ on a bare-metal microcontroller. The controller samples a tri-axial gyroscope every millisecond, computes error dynamics from rigid-body kinematics, and modulates motor pulse-width modulation timers to stabilize the craft against turbulent wind gusts.

**The Digital versus Physical Contrast.** The flight controller exercises absolute physical authority over multi-kilowatt motor drives and operates in continuous feedback with aerodynamic forces. Yet classical aerospace engineering verifies the complete stability envelope using deterministic Lyapunov functions and frequency-domain gain margins, achieving mathematical proofs of stability that modern deep learning models cannot provide.

**The Systems Dilemma.** First, why can this deterministic flight controller be formally certified with bounded worst-case execution time and guaranteed stability margins, whereas a deep reinforcement learning attitude policy with identical sensor inputs cannot? Second, if the classical controller operates with direct actuator authority and tight physical feedback, why does it remain outside the scope of Physical AI? Third, when an engineering team introduces a convolutional neural network front-end to estimate vehicle velocity from optical flow, how does that single learned component destroy the classical stability proof of the entire closed-loop system?

**The Physical AI Insight.** Physical authority and feedback define classical control theory. Physical AI begins only when the control loop incorporates an unspecifiable, learned statistical representation that cannot be verified in closed form.

#### Stress-Test 3: The Microsecond Flash Crash (Learned Model and Delegated Authority, Digital Feedback) {.unnumbered}

**The Scenario.** An autonomous high-frequency market-making algorithm deploys a deep transformer network to predict short-term order flow across equity exchanges. Operating in a co-located datacenter, the system processes streaming order-book telemetry and dispatches limit orders over a $10\text{ Gbps}$ network interface within $3.0\text{ }\mu\text{s}$, executing thousands of trades per minute with delegated authority over millions of dollars in capital.

**The Digital versus Physical Contrast.** The trading model operates with complete execution autonomy, and an inference anomaly can wipe out liquidity in milliseconds. However, the operational medium is discrete and transactional: the system alters electronic database ledgers and network queues rather than physical mass, inertia, or heat.

**The Systems Dilemma.** First, when an unexpected market anomaly causes the trading model to enter a destructive feedback loop, why can the financial exchange engage an electronic circuit breaker to freeze the order book and unwind invalid transactions? Second, why does physical hardware lack an equivalent rollback mechanism when an autonomous robotic manipulator crashes into a workpiece? Third, how does the conservation of momentum and thermodynamic heat dissipation create an irreversible boundary that permanently separates physical machines from high-stakes financial software?

**The Physical AI Insight.** High-stakes digital autonomy risks financial capital, but physical autonomy risks momentum and heat. Digital state transitions can be paused, buffered, and rolled back; kinetic energy transferred to the physical world cannot be recalled.

#### Stress-Test 4: The Shared Autonomy Reflex Gap (The Borderline Case) {.unnumbered}

**The Scenario.** A teleoperated surgical robotic system assists a surgeon during delicate microsurgery. A learned policy provides active haptic guidance, filtering hand tremors and applying gentle repulsive forces to prevent surgical instruments from crossing predefined anatomical boundaries. The surgeon and the learned model simultaneously apply forces to the same surgical tool.

**The Digital versus Physical Contrast.** System designers often assume that keeping a human in the loop preserves ultimate human authority. In physical reality, human neuromuscular reflex latency introduces an inescapable delay of $150\text{ ms}$ to $250\text{ ms}$ before voluntary muscle intervention can arrest an unwanted tool motion.

**The Systems Dilemma.** First, if the surgical assist motor has a mechanical torque ceiling of $0.5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ while the human surgeon can exert $5.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, how does the mechanical impedance ratio determine whether the human or the model holds ultimate physical authority? Second, in a high-speed steer-by-wire vehicle traveling at $30.0\text{ m/s}$, why does a $200\text{ ms}$ human reflex delay grant a learned steering assist policy uninhibited physical authority over $6.0\text{ m}$ of vehicle displacement during a transient inference fault? Third, what precise engineering criteria determine when a shared-autonomy interface crosses the causal boundary into Physical AI?

**The Physical AI Insight.** Authority in shared autonomy is governed by the physics of human reaction time and mechanical impedance. If a learned component can impart un-overridable physical momentum before human neuromuscular reflexes can intervene, the system operates across the causal boundary and demands the full verification rigor of Physical AI.
<!-- END -->

## Summary {#sec-boundary-1-10}

<!-- SECTION 1.10 -->
<!-- claim: The limits are named here but not yet measured, which is Chapter 2's job. -->
<!-- covers: Synthesis of the chapter's core thesis: the causal boundary is a concrete hardware interface where information irreversibly converts into physical energy. -->
<!-- covers: Summary of the four bedrock laws and the tripartite division of Body, Brain, and Nervous System. -->
<!-- covers: Summary of the three physical machine classes and the specific floor limits that bind each. -->
<!-- covers: Bridge to Chapter 2: transitioning from naming physical limits conceptually to measuring and budgeting mass, force, heat, and power on the physical floor. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
The causal boundary is a concrete hardware interface where digital information irreversibly converts into physical energy. It is not a theoretical abstraction or a matter of degree, but a structural line drawn at the switching gates of power inverters, the coils of motor windings, and the poppets of fluid valves. Above this interface, software retains the luxury of idempotency. An inference engine running in a cloud datacenter or a simulation sandbox can drop frames, catch unexpected exceptions, and reset memory registers without altering the external physical state. Below this interface, every bit toggles an electromechanical or thermodynamic state that cannot be undone. When gate drivers energize inductive stator coils, electrical current accelerates mechanical mass against gravity and friction, dissipates resistive heat into copper windings, and modifies the physical environment. In this regime, computation directly shapes its own future sensory inputs ($a_t \to u(t) \to W_{t+1} \to o_{t+1}$). A software stall is not a delayed frame on a display; it is unguided kinetic momentum carrying moving mass forward along an unmanaged trajectory.

Surviving this boundary requires organizing the machine into three distinct subsystems with separate operational responsibilities. The body consists of the linkages, transmissions, motor windings, and fluid conduits that move mass, exert contact force, or regulate a thermodynamic flow. The body obeys classical mechanics and electromagnetism rather than software instructions. The brain comprises the high-capacity learned models running on application processors. The brain provides semantic competence precisely because its weights are learned from data rather than hand-written, yet it remains unaccountable for the exact same reason. Between them sits the nervous system, the deterministic computing substrate that carries signals under strict deadlines dictated by the body. The nervous system executes low-level tracking loops, monitors sensor freshness, and evaluates physical safety invariants on isolated real-time silicon. Because it directly controls the gate drivers and timer peripherals, the nervous system is the only subsystem with the electrical authority to refuse an unsafe proposal and command a controlled stop.

Four bedrock laws govern every interaction across this tripartite structure. First, the law of physical causality and irreversibility establishes that physical actions are permanent; stored kinetic energy and dissipated heat cannot be rolled back with an exception handler. Second, the law of information freshness dictates that physical dynamics evolve continuously without waiting for neural inference. Dynamic stability and obstacle avoidance are bounded by worst-case latency percentiles ($P_{99}$) and sensory age ($\Delta t$), meaning that computational delay is always paid in physical displacement. Third, the law of proposal and permission privilege requires an absolute separation between cognitive intention and motor authority. High-capacity learned models operate strictly as untrusted proposal generators, while deterministic permission supervisors executing in zero-allocation static memory retain exclusive authority over actuator drive stages. Fourth, the law of governed change and defensible release demands that physical policies be qualified through cross-layer fault injection and formal safety cases. Because an acting machine alters its own operational data distribution, unmasked safety interventions corrupt training logs, and empirical demonstrations cannot substitute for verified safety envelopes.

The physical floor manifests differently across the three canonical machine classes, but each class hits an unyielding mechanical or electrical limit. In mobility systems, machines navigate continuous space under the constraints of momentum conservation ($p = mv$) and friction limits. For an autonomous rover traveling at $2.0\text{ m/s}$, an unbudgeted $250\text{ ms}$ inference stall adds $50\text{ cm}$ of unguided displacement before braking can begin, rapidly exhausting available stopping clearance. In contact manipulation, articulated linkages interact with stiff physical environments where contact forces scale steeply with minute positional errors ($F_c \approx k_{\text{c}} \Delta x$). In an analytical example of an arm approaching a steel fixture with contact stiffness $k_{\text{c}} = 1.0 \times 10^5\text{ N/m}$, an overshoot of just $1.5\text{ mm}$ generates $150\text{ N}$ of instantaneous shock force, threatening to chip gear teeth in precision cycloidal drives. In cybernetic energy and process systems, learned policies govern continuous flows of current and fluid. A grid-tied power inverter operating on a $60\text{ Hz}$ utility network faces an electrical cycle of $16.6\text{ ms}$, where an unhandled scheduling delay creates alternating-current phase angle errors that drive destructive surge currents through substation transformers.

The physical limits governing these machines have been named conceptually, but naming a limit does not provide the quantitative ledger required to engineer a physical system. An engineer cannot verify a safety case or configure a real-time permission supervisor using qualitative descriptions alone. Defending a machine against failure requires knowing the exact microsecond waterfall from photon arrival to motor current rise, the thermal capacitance that limits continuous stall torque, the mechanical contact impedance of the workpiece, and the memory bus contention that inflates neural inference tail latencies ($P_{99}$).

Chapter 2 transitions from conceptual boundaries to physical metrology on the hardware floor. By attaching measuring instruments directly to the compute substrate, the power electronics, and the mechanical linkages, we derive the governing equations and measurement disciplines for time, inertia, actuation, energy, and silicon. That quantitative accounting establishes the firm numerical budgets that every subsequent chapter must respect.
